rewritten_text: Weeks passed, and I became more and more absorbed in you. Then something changed. I had portrayed you as Paris in delicate armour, and as Adonis wearing a hunter's cloak and carrying a polished boar spear. Crowned with heavy lotus flowers, you had sat at the prow of Adrian's barge, gazing across the muddy green Nile. You had bent over a quiet pool in a Greek woodland and discovered the wonder of your own face in its silent silver water. All of it had been what art ought to be: unselfconscious, idealized, and distant. Then one day—a fateful day, I sometimes think—I decided to paint a magnificent portrait of you exactly as you are. You would wear your own clothes and belong to your own age, instead of appearing in the costume of vanished centuries. I cannot say whether it was the realism of the approach or the sheer wonder of your personality, presented so directly, without any mist or disguise. But as I worked, I felt that every fleck and layer of colour exposed my secret. I began to fear that other people would discover how I worshipped you. I felt, Dorian, that I had revealed too much, invested too much of myself in the painting. That was when I decided never to exhibit it. You were rather annoyed, but you did not understand everything it meant to me. Harry laughed when I told him. I didn't care. When the picture was finished and I sat alone before it, I felt certain I was right.... A few days later it left my studio. Once I was free of the unbearable fascination of its presence, I began to think I had been foolish to imagine it showed anything beyond your extraordinary good looks and my ability to paint. Even now, I cannot help believing we are mistaken if we think the passion involved in creating something is ever truly visible in the finished work. Art is always more abstract than we suppose. Shape and colour tell us about shape and colour, nothing else. I often think art hides the artist far more completely than it reveals him. So when the offer from Paris came, I decided to make your portrait the central piece of my exhibition. The possibility that you might refuse never entered my mind. Now I see you were right. The painting cannot be shown. Please don't be angry with me, Dorian, because of what I have told you.

"Definitely not," Duff replied.

"And to explain 'yokel' for the ladies, you mean that the person who tried this wasn't a countryman?" Mr. Losberne asked, smiling.

"That's it, sir," Blathers answered. "Is that all you can tell us about the robbery?"

"All of it," said the doctor.

"Then what's this about a boy the servants have been talking about?" Blathers asked.

"Nothing at all," the doctor replied. "One frightened servant decided the boy had something to do with the attempt to break into the house. But the idea is nonsense—utterly ridiculous."

"Should be easy to clear up, then," Duff remarked.

"He's quite right," Blathers said, nodding in agreement. He casually rattled the handcuffs as though they were musical clappers. "Who is this boy? What's his story? Where did he come from? He didn't drop down from the clouds, did he, sir?"

"Certainly not," the doctor said, giving the two ladies a nervous glance. "I know his whole story, but we can talk about it later. First, I suppose you'd like to see where the thieves tried to get in?"

"Of course," Mr. Blathers replied. "We'll look around the property first and question the servants afterward. That's the usual way we work."

Lights were fetched. Blathers and Duff, followed by the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and practically everyone else, went into the small room at the end of the passage and looked out the window. Then they walked around across the lawn and looked in through the window. Next they asked someone to pass out a candle so they could inspect the shutter, then a lantern to follow the footprints, then a pitchfork to poke through the bushes. Everyone watched these proceedings with breathless interest. Afterward the men came back inside, and Mr. Giles and Brittles had to act out their roles in the previous night's events. They gave this dramatic performance about six times. During the first, they disagreed on no more than one important point; during the last, on no more than a dozen. Having reached this splendid result, Blathers and Duff sent everyone out and held a long private discussion. Compared with its secrecy and solemn importance, a meeting of great doctors to discuss the hardest problem in medicine would have seemed like children's play.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced anxiously in the next room as Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with worried expressions.

"Good heavens," he said, finally stopping after many quick turns across the room, "I hardly know what to do."

"Oh, I misunderstood. I thought you said 'anybody,' so I assumed 'anybody' meant—well, anybody. In other words, everyone."

"It does: anybody of noble birth. Preferably someone royal."

"That seems quite reasonable," said the abbot, seizing his chance to soothe the disagreement and prevent disaster. "Surely such an extraordinary gift would hardly be granted to reveal the affairs of people less important than those born close to the heights of greatness. Our King Arthur—"

"You want news of him?" the enchanter interrupted.

"Yes, with the greatest pleasure and gratitude."

At once everyone was full of wonder and fascination again, the hopeless idiots. They watched his spells intently, then looked at me as though saying, 'There! What have you got to say now?' when he announced:

"The king, exhausted from hunting, has been lying in his palace for two hours, deep in dreamless sleep."

"God bless him!" said the abbot, crossing himself. "May that sleep restore his body and soul."

"It might, if he were asleep," I said. "But the king isn't sleeping. He's riding."

Trouble again: two authorities contradicting each other. Nobody knew whom to trust; I still had a little reputation left. The magician's contempt flared up.

"I've encountered many remarkable seers, prophets, and magicians in my life," he said, "but never one who could sit doing nothing and see to the heart of matters without even a spell to assist him."

"You've spent your life in the woods and missed a great deal. I use spells myself, as these good brothers know, but only when the occasion matters."

When it comes to sarcasm, I can generally hold my own. That thrust made the fellow squirm. The abbot asked about the queen and the court, receiving this answer:

"They are all asleep, overcome with fatigue just like the king."

I said:

"That's simply another lie. Half of them are enjoying themselves. The queen and the other half aren't sleeping; they're riding. Perhaps you could stretch yourself a little and tell us where the king, queen, and everyone riding with them at this moment are going?"

"As I said, they are sleeping now. Tomorrow they will ride, because they are setting out toward the sea."

"And where will they be at evening prayers the day after tomorrow?"

"Far north of Camelot, with half their journey behind them."

"That's another lie, by a distance of a hundred and fifty miles.
